sites.s: 18th-century pearling town · World Heritage
sites.te: The town that pearls built
sites.se: A walled trading town of 6,000 to 9,000 people, burned in 1811 and buried by sand
sites.sa: مدينة تجارية مسوّرة سكنها 6 إلى 9 آلاف إنسان، أُحرقت عام 1811 ودفنتها الرمال
sites.desc: A pearling and trading town founded in the 1760s on the north-west coast, 85 km from Doha. The late 18th-century town wall forms a 2.5 km arc from shore to shore around a 60 ha site that may have held 6,000–9,000 people; a palatial compound of 110 × 100 m has nine courtyards. Forces loyal to the Sultan of Muscat burned the town in 1811, a later town covered about 20% of the area, and the site was abandoned by the early 20th century. Qal'at Murair, a fortified settlement inland, stayed occupied until Al Zubarah Fort was built in 1938. Inscribed on the World Heritage List on 22 June 2013, Qatar's first.
sites.sig: The best-preserved example of an 18th–19th-century Gulf merchant town, with its street plan, souq, houses and fishing harbours intact under the sand.
sites.ex: Qatar Museums with the University of Copenhagen (Qatar Islamic Archaeology and Heritage Project), 2009 onwards; Qatari excavations of the souq in the 1980s
disc: 2.5 km town wall from shore to shore

sites.s: Largest rock-art site in Qatar
sites.te: Boats cut into the rock
sites.se: Rows of cup marks and 141 boats carved into a coastal ridge
sites.sa: صفوف من الحفر الفنجانية و141 قاربًا محفورة في ضلع ساحلي
sites.desc: About 900 carvings across 580 numbered sites on a low ridge 4.8 km south of Fuwairit, discovered in 1961 by a Danish team under Holger Kapel and recorded by Hans Kapel in 1974. Cup-and-ring marks are the most common motif, with animals (ostriches, turtles, fish) and boats: 124 plan drawings and 17 elevation drawings, the only recorded boat carvings in Qatar. Dating is debated: Facey (1987) put the earliest boat drawings at the 11th century AD on the evidence of rudders, Nayeem (1998) suggested the 3rd century BC, and a 2012 dating study found its oldest sample under 300 years old. Nearby habitation mounds hold pottery of the 10th–11th centuries.
sites.sig: The richest open-air rock-art site on the Gulf coast, and a rare record of the dhows of the pearling age.
sites.ex: Danish Archaeological Expedition (H. Kapel) 1961; H. Kapel 1974; de Cardi 1973–74

sites.s: Kassite purple-dye workshop
sites.te: Three million crushed shells
sites.se: The oldest known purple-dye works, on an island of mangroves
sites.sa: أقدم مصنع معروف للصبغة الأرجوانية، على جزيرة من القرم
sites.desc: A 1.67 km² island in the bay of Al Khor, 50 km north of Doha, joined to the shore by a causeway at low water. Dilmun-period pottery (c. 2000–1750 BC) links it to Bahrain; in the Kassite period (c. 1400–1100 BC) it became a purple-dye works, with about 3,000,000 crushed murex shells (Hexaplex trunculus) and Kassite potsherds, claimed as the earliest known production of shellfish purple. Sasanian and late Islamic material shows later use. First studied systematically in 1976 by the French mission under Jacques Tixier, then by Carter and Killick. Avicennia mangroves line its east and south-east shores.
sites.sig: The earliest industrial-scale purple-dye site known, tying Qatar to the Kassite kings of Babylon and Dilmun.
sites.ex: Mission Archéologique Française à Qatar (J. Tixier) 1976; Carter & Killick (2014)
refs: Carter, R. & Killick, R. (2014). Al-Khor Island: investigating coastal exploitation in Bronze Age Qatar. Moonrise Press.

sites.s: Oldest settlement in Qatar
sites.te: The first campfires
sites.se: People lived here 7,500 years ago, until something sudden ended it
sites.sa: عاش الناس هنا قبل 7,500 عام، حتى أنهى ذلك حدث مفاجئ
sites.desc: A Neolithic settlement on the north-west coast with occupation from about 7,500 years ago, excavated over three seasons to 2013 by the Qatar National Historic Environment Record project of the University of Birmingham and Qatar Museums (co-director Richard Cuttler). Flint scatters and pottery mark the earliest phase; settlement appears to have ended abruptly shortly after 4,500 years ago, possibly in a high-energy event such as a tsunami.
sites.sig: Qatar's oldest known settlement, contemporary with the Ubaid-period villages of Kuwait and Saudi Arabia across the Gulf.
sites.ex: QNHER project, University of Birmingham and Qatar Museums (R. Cuttler, P. Spencer), 2010–2013
refs: Gulf Times (13 July 2013). Wadi Debayan offers detailed and rich story of human occupation.

sites.s: Abbasid village with the oldest fort
sites.te: A village of 250 houses
sites.se: An Abbasid village that traded pearls for glazed pots from Basra and Samarra
sites.sa: قرية عباسية قايضت اللؤلؤ بأوانٍ مزجّجة من البصرة وسامراء
sites.desc: A 9th-century village 4 km from the west coast and 15 km north of Dukhan: 250 ruined houses, two mosques and a rectangular fort with a central courtyard and twelve rooms, the oldest known fort in Qatar. Of 6,948 potsherds, most date to 805–885 AD, with glazed wares from Susa, Basra or Samarra and no Chinese porcelain; at least 18% of the common pots had been repaired. Discovered by Geoffrey Bibby's Danish team in 1959, excavated by C. Hardy-Guilbert in 1984 and Alexandrine Guérin in 2009. Abandoned in the late 9th century as the Qarmatian revolt began.
sites.sig: The clearest picture of early Islamic village life in Qatar, and evidence of pearl-for-pottery trade with Iraq.
sites.ex: Danish expedition (G. Bibby) 1959; French missions 1984 and 2009
refs: Guérin, A. & Al-Naimi, F. (2010). Preliminary pottery study: Murwab horizon in progress, ninth century AD, Qatar. Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 40.

sites.s: Watchtowers of Umm Salal Mohammed
sites.te: Towers that watched the moon
sites.se: Built to guard a rainwater valley, watch the sea and sight the Ramadan moon
sites.sa: بُنيت لحراسة وادٍ لمياه الأمطار، ومراقبة البحر، ورؤية هلال رمضان
sites.desc: Two watchtowers of coral rock and limestone with mud mortar, 16 m high with walls about 1 m thick at the base, on the low hill of Jebel Lusail at Umm Salal Mohammed, 15 km north of Doha and 10 km from the coast. Built in the late 19th century and renovated in 1910 by Sheikh Mohammed bin Jassim Al Thani, they guarded the rawda, a depression that collected rainwater, watched for Ottoman troops and approaching ships, and were used to sight the new moon of Ramadan. Restored in 2003 and now a museum.
sites.sig: A rare surviving example of Qatar's pre-oil defensive architecture, tied to water rather than to a coast.
sites.ex: Qatar Museums (restoration 2003)
disc: Walls 1 m thick of coral rock and limestone
Rawda rainwater depression below the towers

sites.s: Eroded Eocene mesas
sites.el: Abarug member: 2 m limestone over 10 m marl
sites.te: Tables and mushrooms of stone
sites.se: Wind and salt carved mesas and mushroom rocks from a layered Eocene sea floor
sites.sa: نحتت الرياح والملح موائد وصخور فطر من قاع بحر إيوسيني مطبّق
sites.desc: A peninsula north of Dukhan on the west coast, defined by the half-moon Bay of Zekreet and lying inside the Al Reem Biosphere Reserve. Foothills, mesas and gypsum plateaux are carved from the Abarug member of the Eocene Dammam Formation: an upper 2 m of dull dolomitic limestone over 10 m of brightly coloured dolomitic marl, so that the resistant cap protects pillars and mushroom rocks as the soft marl erodes. Ostriches, gazelles and reintroduced oryx roam the Ras Abrouq headland, and flamingos feed in the bay. Richard Serra's East-West/West-East steel plates stand in a valley here. Tourism has caused litter and vegetation damage.
sites.sig: Qatar's most striking natural landscape and a clear lesson in differential erosion of the Eocene sea floor.
sites.ex: Qatar Natural History Group; UNESCO Doha (Al Reem studies)
disc: Hard 2 m limestone cap over soft 10 m marl

sites.s: Qatar’s first oil, 1940
sites.p: Jurassic reservoirs under an Eocene fold
sites.el: Anticline 80 km long · well 1,733 m deep
sites.te: The hill of smoke
sites.se: An 80 km fold at the surface led drillers to Jurassic oil 1,733 m down
sites.sa: طيّة بطول 80 كم على السطح قادت الحفّارين إلى نفط جوراسي على عمق 1,733 م
sites.desc: A north–south anticline about 80 km long and up to 8 km wide on the west coast, whose Middle Eocene limestone limbs dip 2–10° with about 90 m of surface closure; the hazy hills were called Jabal Dukhan, the hill of smoke. Dukhan No. 1 was spudded in October 1938 and completed in January 1940 at 1,733 m, flowing about 4,480 barrels a day from Upper Jurassic limestone (the Zekrit Formation, equivalent to the Arab Formation) rather than the expected Cretaceous. The first cargo, 80,000 tons, left Umm Said on 31 December 1949. Non-associated gas was found in the Permian Khuff Formation at about 3,000 m in 1959–60, with production from 1978.
sites.sig: The structure that made modern Qatar, and a textbook case of surface geology pointing to deep oil.
sites.ex: Petroleum Development (Qatar) Ltd, 1938–1940; QatarEnergy
disc: Discovery well completed January 1940 at 1,733 m
refs: Sorkhabi, R. (2010). The Qatar oil discoveries. GEO ExPro.

sites.s: The fold that lifted the peninsula
sites.dr: Rocks 56 million years old to recent
sites.te: Why Qatar is above the sea
sites.se: A long, gentle arch of the Arabian plate holds the whole peninsula out of the water
sites.sa: قوس طويل لطيف في الصفيحة العربية يرفع شبه الجزيرة كلها فوق الماء
sites.desc: Qatar sits on the eastern stable shelf of the Arabian Plate, lifted by the Qatar–South Fars Arch, a regional NNE–SSW anticline bounded to the north by the Zagros belt. The surface is mostly Lower Eocene to Pleistocene limestone and dolostone with marl, shale, clay and gypsum, plus Upper Miocene–Pliocene gravels and conglomerates; the highest point is 103 m in the south-west, and aeolian dunes cover about 12% of the country. The same arch carries the Dukhan field and the offshore North Field.
sites.sig: The single structure that explains Qatar's existence, its flatness, its caves and its hydrocarbons.
sites.ex: Al-Awah & Matter (2023); Qatar geological surveys
disc: Peninsula lifted on a NNE–SSW arch
refs: Al-Awah, H. & Matter, W. S. (2023). Physicochemical characterization and origin of aeolian sand dunes in southeastern Qatar. Advances in Geosciences 63, 1–13.

sites.s: Gypsum cave that glows
sites.dr: Limestone 40 – 50 million years old; cave younger
sites.te: The cave that glows
sites.se: Fibrous gypsum crystals light a 40 m sinkhole in the central desert
sites.sa: بلورات جبس ليفية تضيء دحلًا بعمق 40 م في الصحراء الوسطى
sites.desc: A sinkhole cave about 40 km south-west of Doha near Rawdat Rashid, 40 m deep (at least 100 m by one account) with an entrance of about 12 × 4.5 m. Its fibrous gypsum crystals, derived from the Lower Dammam and Rus Formations, give the interior a faint phosphorescent glow; the surrounding Eocene limestone is 40–50 million years old and the cave formed later by dissolution, part of the Middle Pleistocene karst of Qatar. Fenced, free to enter and rehabilitated in 2022 with paths and a cave map.
sites.sig: The deepest accessible dahl in Qatar and the best place to see the gypsum that underlies the peninsula.
sites.ex: Ministry of Environment and Climate Change (rehabilitation 2022)
disc: Fibrous gypsum with a phosphorescent glow
refs: Sadiq, A. M. & Nasir, S. J. (2002). Middle Pleistocene karst evolution in the State of Qatar, Arabian Gulf. Journal of Cave and Karst Studies 64(2), 132–139.

sites.n: Mesaieed Dunes and Khor Al Adaid Sands
sites.s: Mobile dunes marching to the sea
sites.dr: Active today; sand supply nearly exhausted
sites.te: Dunes on their last journey
sites.se: Wind drives the sand south-east into the Inland Sea, and no new sand arrives
sites.sa: تدفع الريح الرمال جنوبًا شرقًا إلى البحر الداخلي، ولا تصل رمال جديدة
sites.desc: Mobile barchan and parabolic dunes south of Mesaieed, driven by the north-north-westerly shamal toward the Inland Sea and eastern Saudi Arabia. Vegetation cover is 0–1%, far below the 8% that normally checks wind erosion, and the sand supply is described as limited to exhausted: at current rates the dunes could be gone in roughly 500–1,500 years. Dunes cover about 12% of Qatar and are best developed here in the south.
sites.sig: A dune field with an expiry date, and the sand that gives Khor Al Adaid its spectacle.
sites.ex: UNESCO Doha (B. Boer); Al-Awah & Matter (2023)

sites.s: Tidal inland sea · UNESCO tentative list
sites.te: Where the desert meets the sea
sites.se: A tidal lagoon with no equal, ringed by dunes that spill into the water
sites.sa: بحيرة مدّية لا نظير لها، تحيط بها كثبان تنهال في الماء
sites.desc: A tidal embayment in the south-east about 15 km north–south and up to 12 km east–west, linked to the Gulf by a channel of about 10 km, submitted to UNESCO's Tentative List on 18 March 2008 under natural criteria (vii) and (viii). Barchan and parabolic dunes reach and spill into the sea; inland and coastal sabkhas prograde seaward under the shamal, salt hummocks record Holocene sea-level change, and dolomite precipitates beneath the surface. Dugongs, turtles, corals and seagrass live in the lagoon, ospreys nest on islets, migrant waterfowl winter here, and Arabian gazelles use the shore.
sites.sig: The only lagoon system of its kind, where active dunes, sabkhas and a tidal sea meet in one protected landscape.
sites.ex: Ministry of Environment and Climate Change; UNESCO Tentative List ref. 5317
disc: Dunes spilling directly into tidal water
Dolomite forming today beneath the sabkha

sites.s: UNESCO biosphere reserve
sites.te: A tenth of the country, kept wild
sites.se: Oryx and gazelle on the limestone plains of the north-west
sites.sa: المها والغزال على سهول الشمال الغربي الجيرية
sites.desc: A semi-arid reserve of 120,000 ha in the north-west, about 65 km from Doha, established in 2005 and recognised by UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere programme in 2007. It is an inhabited landscape of limestone plains, mesas and coast, including the Zekreet peninsula and Ras Abrouq, with Arabian oryx and gazelles among its wildlife and vegetation valued by local communities.
sites.sig: One of 24 UNESCO biosphere reserves in the Middle East and the frame for Qatar's wildlife reintroductions.

sites.s: One of the largest whale shark gatherings
sites.te: A hundred giants in one square kilometre
sites.ta: مئة عملاق في كيلومتر مربع واحد
sites.se: Whale sharks gather around oil platforms to feed on tuna eggs
sites.sa: تتجمع أقراش الحوت حول منصات النفط لتأكل بيض التونة
sites.desc: Around the Al Shaheen oil field about 90 km offshore in 60 m of water, whale sharks gather from April to September with a peak from May to August. In 2011 densities reached 100 sharks per km², about 100 were counted on 9 July, 178 in June, and groups of 40 were seen from the platforms; the sharks averaged 6.9 m long and most were male. They feed at the surface on fish eggs identified by DNA as mackerel tuna, which spawn around the platforms as if around fish-aggregating devices.
sites.sig: One of the largest whale shark aggregations known anywhere, created by an unexpected link between oil platforms and spawning tuna.
sites.ex: Qatar Ministry of Environment, Maersk Oil Research and Technology Centre (Robinson et al. 2013)
refs: Robinson, D. P., Jaidah, M. Y., Jabado, R. W. et al. (2013). Whale sharks, Rhincodon typus, aggregate around offshore platforms in Qatari waters of the Arabian Gulf to feed on fish spawn. PLoS ONE 8(3), e58255.

sites.s: Hawksbill nesting beach
sites.te: Where the hawksbills come home
sites.se: 219 turtles nested in 2025 and 8,213 hatchlings reached the sea
sites.sa: عشّشت 219 سلحفاة عام 2025 ووصل 8,213 فرخًا إلى البحر
sites.desc: The main hawksbill turtle nesting beach of Qatar, designated in 2020 and closed to the public each nesting season from the end of March to July. In 2025, 219 turtles nested on eight beaches (Fuwairit, Ras Rakan, Ras Laffan, Sharawa, Umm Tais, Al Ghariyah, Al Maroona and Al Khor), nests were relocated to Fuwairit and Ras Laffan, and 8,213 hatchlings were released; more than 60,000 hatchlings have been released in five years. The Hawksbill Turtle Conservation Project has run since 2003 with QatarEnergy and Qatar University's Environmental Science Centre.
sites.sig: The northern Gulf's most important hawksbill rookery, in one of the hottest nesting environments on Earth.
sites.ex: Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, QatarEnergy, Qatar University ESC

sites.s: Largest mangrove forest in Qatar
sites.te: Half of Qatar’s mangroves
sites.se: A grey-green forest in the tide, storing carbon and sheltering fish
sites.sa: غابة رمادية خضراء في المدّ، تخزّن الكربون وتؤوي الأسماك
sites.desc: The largest mangrove habitat in Qatar, north of Al Khor on the east coast: more than 7 km² of the country's roughly 14 km² of mangroves lie inside the Al Thakhira Reserve, with other stands at Al Khor, Al Wakra, Mesaieed, Al Alia Island, Fuwairit, Al Ruwais, Al Arish and Al Jamil. The Ministry of Environment runs afforestation and restoration programmes based on studies of tide, soil and salinity, citing a global estimate of about 3,754 tonnes of CO₂ stored per hectare including soils.
sites.sig: A nursery for fish and a carbon store on a coast that has lost most of its natural shoreline.
sites.ex: Ministry of Environment and Climate Change

sites.s: Record herds on the seagrass
sites.te: Five hundred in a square kilometre
sites.se: The largest dugong herds outside Australia graze off the west coast
sites.sa: أكبر قطعان الأطوم خارج أستراليا ترعى قبالة الساحل الغربي
sites.desc: In the shallow seagrass waters off west and north-west Qatar, helicopter surveys in late 2015 and early 2016 counted 508 dugongs within an area under 1 km², with cow–calf pairs 9.9% of the group, and two foraging herds of 226 and 166 in December 2015. The waters between Qatar and Bahrain form an Important Marine Mammal Area of 10,676 km² holding the world's second-largest dugong population; winter surveys in 2004 had recorded groups of 577 and 97.
sites.sig: The clearest evidence that the Gulf's dugong population persists at the size first recorded in the 1980s.
sites.ex: Marshall et al. (2018); Preen (2004)

sites.s: Fort of the 1893 battle
sites.te: The day the Ottomans turned back
sites.se: A small square fort where Sheikh Jassim’s men defeated an Ottoman force in 1893
sites.sa: قلعة مربعة صغيرة هزم فيها رجال الشيخ جاسم قوة عثمانية عام 1893
sites.desc: A fort in Al Wajbah, about 15 km west of Doha, thought to date from the late 18th or 19th century. In 1893, after Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed Al Thani stopped paying taxes to the Ottomans, a contingent sent against him was defeated here and retreated to Doha, three hours away; the battle is remembered as the founding moment of modern Qatar. Restored to its original state in 1990 by the Museums and Archaeology Department, which removed later alterations.
sites.sig: The site of the battle that secured Al Thani rule and the independence of the peninsula from Ottoman control.
sites.ex: National Council for Culture, Arts and Heritage (restoration 1990)

sites.s: Fortified coastal town of the 16th–18th centuries · Qatar Museums heritage site
sites.el: Largest fort in Qatar · 2.25 ha with its outer wall
sites.te: The fort that grew eight times
sites.se: A 2.5 km coastal town with the largest fort in Qatar, two mosques, a boatyard and warehouses, deserted when its people moved to Al Zubarah
sites.sa: مدينة ساحلية بطول 2.5 كم تضم أكبر قلعة في قطر ومسجدين وورشة سفن ومخازن، هُجرت حين انتقل أهلها إلى الزبارة
sites.desc: A ruined town on the north-west coast between Al Zubarah and Al Ruwais, stretching about 2.5 km along the shore, with a central square fort of two complexes covering about 2.25 ha including its outer wall. The fort was built in three phases, the last expansion making it eight times its original size; one solid corner tower about 4 m tall may have held a cannon. Discovered by Beatrice de Cardi's British mission in 1973, it was excavated in 2008–2014 by the University of Wales (Lampeter/Trinity Saint David) under Andrew Petersen with the Qatar Museums Authority, uncovering a seafront mosque rebuilt five times, an eight-room warehouse with a date press, a boat workshop, a well and a tomb. Finds include Iranian glazed pottery of the late 16th–early 17th century, 18th-century Chinese ceramics and a 5 cm bone plaque carved with an oryx, about 300 years old. Local informants told Lorimer the town was deserted around the 1760s when residents moved to Al Zubarah.
sites.sig: The largest fort in Qatar and the best-studied of the pre-Zubarah coastal towns, showing a trading community whose pottery came from Iran and China.
sites.ex: Beatrice de Cardi (1973); University of Wales Trinity Saint David (A. Petersen) with Qatar Museums Authority, 2008–2014
disc: Fort of 2.25 ha, enlarged eight times over
Bone plaque carved with an oryx, c. 300 years old

sites.s: 17th–18th-century fortified village north of Al Zubarah
sites.el: Village of c. 50 ha · 700 m along the shore
sites.te: The village before Zubarah
sites.se: A fishing village with a fort, a mosque and 303 rock carvings, at its peak before its famous neighbour
sites.sa: قرية صيد فيها قلعة ومسجد و303 نقوش صخرية، بلغت ذروتها قبل جارتها الشهيرة
sites.desc: A deserted village on a shallow bay 3 km north of Al Zubarah, covering about 50 ha and extending some 700 m along the coast and 200 m inland. Excavations and documents put its peak in the 17th–18th centuries, probably before Zubarah; Lorimer counted about 150 inhabitants, mostly fishermen, in 1904, and it was occupied by Qatari forces in July 1937. Qal'at Freiha, a fortified building with corner towers, store rooms and date presses, was excavated and conserved in 2005; from 2009 the Qatar Islamic Archaeology and Heritage Project of Qatar Museums and the University of Copenhagen mapped the site and excavated the central mosque (mihrab, minbar, washing well and courtyard), houses and middens. Stone fishing weights, fish bones and tidal fish traps show a marine economy. Bibby and Glob recorded several hundred cup-marks 5–23 cm wide here in 1956, and Hans Kapel catalogued 303 carvings in 1983.
sites.sig: A complete small coastal settlement of the pearling age, older than Al Zubarah, excavated as part of the World Heritage site's hinterland.

sites.s: Early Islamic workshop settlement · Landscapes of Faith excavation
sites.el: 24 structures · one of only 5 large clustered sites of the period
sites.te: Abbasid workshops in the desert
sites.se: Paired rooms with plastered basins and platforms, probably for washing and dyeing wool 1,200 years ago
sites.sa: غرف متجاورة بأحواض ومنصات مجصّصة، ربما لغسل الصوف وصبغه قبل 1,200 عام
sites.desc: An abandoned village 1.5 km south-west of Freiha with 24 structures including two mosques, a fort and the masonry well that Lorimer recorded in 1908, and an Early Islamic site excavated since winter 2022 by the Qatar Museums Department of Archaeology's Landscapes of Faith project directed by Robert Carter. Occupation is dated by pottery and glass to about 780–830 AD. The main building was planned as three production units of paired rooms with gypsum-plastered basins and platforms, drains through the walls and no kitchens, resembling small industrial units; the team proposes textile work such as washing and dyeing wool. Most pottery was imported from southern Iraq, with wares from Iran, Bahrain, Oman and a few pieces from China; food remains include dates, wheat, barley, dugong and large quantities of pearl oysters. Qatar has more than 30 known sites of the 7th–9th centuries, but only five large clustered ones like Ain Mohammed and nearby Mesaika (c. 750–780 AD).
sites.sig: Evidence that early Abbasid Qatar had purpose-built manufacturing settlements supplied from Iraq, not just villages.

sites.s: Largest Ubaid-period site in Qatar · west coast
sites.te: Sixty fires by the sea
sites.se: A seasonal camp of fishers and hunters where painted Ubaid pottery from Mesopotamia was found in 1961
sites.sa: مخيم موسمي لصيادين وجامعي ثمار عُثر فيه عام 1961 على فخار عبيدي مزخرف من بلاد الرافدين
sites.desc: A Neolithic settlement on the west coast of Qatar, described as the most extensive Ubaid site in the country. It was discovered in 1961 by the Danish team of Holger Kapel, the largest of several flint sites they excavated in 1960–64, and a British team then identified the potsherds as Ubaid; Beatrice de Cardi's team worked here in 1978. Finds include many painted Ubaid sherds, quern fragments, flint scrapers, blades and arrowheads, a carnelian bead and three fragments of red non-Ubaid pottery, along with nearly sixty hearths and postholes for tents or huts. It is interpreted as a seasonal encampment of a hunting, fishing and gathering group that returned repeatedly; the stone tools match Arabian rather than Mesopotamian traditions. A village for Dukhan oil workers was founded on the spot in 1956.
sites.sig: Qatar's principal link to the Ubaid world of southern Mesopotamia, showing seaborne contact across the Arabian Gulf in the Neolithic.

sites.s: Cairn field of hundreds of tombs · Bronze Age to Sasanian
sites.el: Mounds 3–6 m across · hundreds, possibly thousands
sites.te: Mother of water, field of cairns
sites.se: Low stone mounds over graves spread across a well-watered depression, dug by Danish, Japanese and German teams
sites.sa: ركامات حجرية منخفضة فوق قبور تنتشر في منخفض غني بالماء، نقّب فيها دنماركيون ويابانيون وألمان
sites.desc: An archaeological area on the west coast about 80 km north-west of Doha, named for its freshwater wells; Lorimer in 1908 noted good masonry wells and a ruined fort built by a Shaikh of Bahrain. Most activity is concentrated in the Mleiha depression of about 25 km², where burial mounds 3–6 m in diameter and 10 cm to 1 m high are capped with limestone, many damaged by robbers, weathering and off-road driving. Bibby and Glob found 50 cairns in 1957, one with a stone cist, and dated pit-fired pottery and alabaster bowl sherds to about 3000 BC by comparison with Bahrain; de Cardi's team found Indian red polished ware and glazed pottery of the Sasanian period (3rd–7th century AD); a Japanese mission (Konishi, Gotoh, Akashi, 1988–91) excavated cists with beads, bronze rings and pottery and proposed a date around the 1st century BC–AD; a German survey led by Juergen Schreiber in 2008 estimated hundreds, possibly thousands, of tombs and saw them as the work of nomads.
sites.sig: Qatar's largest ancient cemetery, whose contested dates span three millennia of nomadic life on the peninsula.

sites.s: Desert fort over a 35-foot well · 17th–19th century
sites.dr: Village from the 10th century · fort 17th – 19th century
sites.te: A fort to guard a well
sites.se: Four towers around a courtyard, built of coral and limestone where rainwater gathered in the wadi
sites.sa: أربعة أبراج حول فناء، بُنيت من المرجان والحجر الجيري حيث يتجمع ماء المطر في الوادي
sites.desc: A fort near the abandoned village of Ath Thaqab in Al Shamal, about 110 km from Doha and 4.8 km from Al Khuwayr. Its name comes from thaghab, the water that lies in channels after rain. The fort is square with three circular towers and one rectangular tower, a central courtyard with stairs, a bent entrance and buildings for storing and processing dates, built of rough coral and limestone blocks bonded with mud mortar; it is dated between the 17th and 19th centuries, while archaeological evidence suggests the village was inhabited from the 10th century. Lorimer in 1908 recorded a well about 35 feet (11 m) deep west of the fort whose good water was fetched by the people of Al Khuwayr. In July 1937 a force sent by Sheikh Abdullah Al Thani took the fort and confiscated 40 rifles from residents.
sites.sig: One of the chain of northern desert forts built to protect wells, the scarcest resource of the pearling-age villages.

sites.s: Mid-18th-century well fort · ISESCO heritage list 2021
sites.dr: Mid-18th century (coins of 749–846 AD also found)
sites.te: The fort named for wells
sites.se: A 28 by 22 m mud-and-limestone fort with a well inside, restored in 1988 and again in 2020–21
sites.sa: قلعة من الطين والحجر الجيري بأبعاد 28 × 22 م وبداخلها بئر، رُممت عام 1988 ثم في 2020–2021
sites.desc: A rectangular fort of mud and limestone, 28 × 22 m, on the road between Al Zubarah and Madinat Al Shamal about 110–115 km from Doha, with three rectangular corner towers and one cylindrical tower, narrow windowless rooms on three sides of a courtyard and a single entrance in the south wall. Its name refers to wells, and it was built to protect a freshwater well inside the fort for the surrounding village. Archaeological evidence suggests the mid-18th century, when Al Zubarah flourished, although coins of 749–846 AD were also found. First restored in 1988, it was conserved by Qatar Museums from October 2020 to September 2021, with a roof rebuilt in traditional danchal, basgil and manghrour, and in June 2021 it joined ISESCO's List of Heritage in the Islamic World.
sites.sig: A well-preserved example of the water-guarding desert forts of northern Qatar, now one of three Qatari sites on the ISESCO heritage list.

sites.s: 33 km Miocene ridge · type area of the Dam Formation
sites.te: A ridge of gypsum and stromatolites
sites.se: The highest ground in southern Qatar, three rock layers of a Miocene sea, mined for gypsum in 1948
sites.sa: أعلى أرض في جنوب قطر، ثلاث طبقات صخرية من بحر ميوسيني، استُخرج منها الجبس عام 1948
sites.desc: A ridge in southern Qatar running 33 km from south-east to north-west parallel to the west coast, rising to about 90 m. It exposes three members of the Miocene Dam Formation: the Salwa Member (about 27 m) at the base, the gypsum-rich Nakhsh Member (about 33 m), the only member with stromatolites, and the Abu Samrah Member (about 6 m) on top. Weathering of soft clays has collapsed the lower limestone into dens used by foxes and hyenas, caves first surveyed by Peter Whybrow in 1983–84. After a 1947 survey, British authorities had the ridge mined for gypsum, with a railway to Umm Bab; output reached 650 tons in the second half of 1949, though geologist Jacques Leblanc notes the mountain shows no clear signs of exploitation.
sites.sig: The best exposure of Qatar's Miocene sea-floor layers, and a landmark that shaped the geography of the south-west.

sites.s: Inland salt flat below sea level · Holocene evaporites
sites.el: 107 km² basin · 1–2 m below sea level
sites.te: A sea that dried into salt
sites.se: A 107 km² hollow between the Dukhan anticline and the Qatar Arch where gypsum, halite and anhydrite still crystallise
sites.sa: منخفض مساحته 107 كم² بين طيّة دخان المحدبة وقوس قطر، ما يزال يتبلور فيه الجبس والهاليت والأنهيدريت
sites.desc: An inland sabkha on the west coast south of Dukhan, filling a synclinal depression between the Dukhan anticline to the west and the Qatar Arch to the east. Holocene sediments cover a structural low of 107 km², mostly 1–2 m below sea level, 4–6 m thick and up to 12 m, over Eocene carbonates; a 12 km² salt flat in the north-east is the youngest lake deposit. Gypsum is the dominant mineral (20–30%), with halite 8–11% and anhydrite about 5%, and prismatic gypsum up to 7 m thick records a saline lake at the centre. Sea-level reconstruction shows an early Holocene marine embayment flooding from the north that became ever more restricted into evaporite lakes; Qatar University work dates the sabkha to the last 5,000 years. Qatar has 78 inland sabkha patches covering about 205 km² and 42 coastal sabkhas totalling 701 km².
sites.sig: A natural laboratory for how evaporites form, studied by Bristol and ExxonMobil Research Qatar as a model for ancient salt-bearing rocks.

sites.s: Largest coastal salt flat in Qatar · 55 km long
sites.te: A lagoon filled with sand
sites.se: A former lagoon south of Mesaieed, now a gypsum-cemented plain that grew seaward over six thousand years
sites.sa: بحيرة شاطئية قديمة جنوب مسيعيد صارت سهلًا متماسكًا بالجبس تقدّم نحو البحر على مدى ستة آلاف عام
sites.desc: The largest coastal sabkha in Qatar, on the east coast just south of Mesaieed, roughly 55 km long and 4–14 km wide, formed from a former lagoon that filled with wind-blown siliciclastic sand. Bristol and ExxonMobil Research Qatar geologists describe it as a prograding coastal plain 4–6 km wide whose Holocene wedge is 3–6 m thick, reaching about 15 m at the coast, over Eocene limestones and dolomites. Gypsum is the main diagenetic mineral, 20–50% of the sediment over several km², with calcite, dolomite, anhydrite and halite minor; gypsum cement is pervasive in the inland part (about 6,000 years old), restricted to crusts in the centre (about 4,000 years) and largely absent at the coast (about 2,000 years). Evaporative pumping of groundwater from the Eocene aquifer is the main source of salts, and the gypsum helps stabilise a surface that vehicles can cross when dry.
sites.sig: A textbook example of a prograding coastal sabkha, showing how a shoreline moved seaward and cemented itself with gypsum.

sites.s: Collapse sinkhole in a Doha park · tidal pool inside
sites.p: Karst in Eocene Rus and Dammam formations
sites.el: 60 m long · entrance 12 m wide, 9 m high
sites.te: A cave in the middle of the city
sites.se: A collapse doline whose brackish pool rises and falls 30 cm with the tide, one of more than 9,700 depressions in Qatar
sites.sa: حفرة انهيارية ترتفع بركتها المالحة وتنخفض 30 سم مع المد والجزر، واحدة من أكثر من 9,700 منخفض في قطر
sites.desc: A collapse doline, or sinkhole, fenced in the north-east corner of Dahl Al Hamam Park in central Doha, about 60 m long with a portal 12 m wide and 9 m high and a staircase of about 20 steps down the cliff. Brackish water at its sides rises and falls about 30 cm with the tides, suggesting a connection to the sea; divers explored underwater passages behind the pool in 2016, and a 2016 gravity survey by Howari, Aldouri and Sadiq found a strong negative anomaly marking water-filled caves linked to the Arabian Gulf. Lorimer in 1908 called it Dahail and noted a rocky pool of good water. It belongs to a karst landscape of more than 9,700 depressions in Qatar, formed by subsurface dissolution of limestone, dolomite, gypsum and anhydrite of the Eocene Rus and Dammam formations under wet Middle Pleistocene conditions, followed by subsidence. Pigeons nesting inside gave the cave, and the district, its name.
sites.sig: The most accessible of Qatar's dahl caves, and a reminder that the capital stands on dissolving Eocene rock.

sites.s: Qatar's first Arabian oryx sanctuary · 1979
sites.te: Where the white oryx came back
sites.se: A 12 km² reserve founded in 1979 for the national animal, declared extinct in the wild in 1972
sites.sa: محمية مساحتها 12 كم² أُسست عام 1979 للحيوان الوطني الذي أُعلن انقراضه في البرية عام 1972
sites.desc: A 12 km² reserve at Al Shahaniya, about 45 km from Doha, designated in 1979 as a sanctuary for the Arabian oryx and one of the first nature reserves established by the State. The oryx were brought from Muaither farm by Sheikh Abdul Rahman bin Saud Al Thani, and Sheikh Jassim bin Hamad Al Thani was the first to give the animals special attention there; the reserve also holds a pen for North African red-necked ostriches. The species had been declared extinct in the wild in October 1972 after poachers killed the last herd in Oman; Sheikh Faisal bin Qassim Al Thani's 1967 expedition caught five animals in Oman that founded Qatar's Royal Herd. The IUCN moved the oryx from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2011, and the animals have since spread to more than 10 protected areas in Qatar, with up to 10,000 wild and semi-wild oryx estimated in the country.
sites.sig: The starting point of Qatar's oryx recovery, one of the Gulf's most successful returns of an animal from extinction in the wild.

sites.s: 54 km² oryx and gazelle reserve in the south-west · 1997
sites.te: A thousand oryx among the dunes
sites.se: Sandy plains south-east of Abu Samra where oryx and reem gazelles are bred for release
sites.sa: سهول رملية جنوب شرق أبو سمرة تُربّى فيها المها وغزلان الريم لإطلاقها
sites.desc: A reserve of about 54 km² in south-west Qatar, south-east of Abu Samra, officially opened in 1997 to resettle the Arabian oryx, the reem (sand) gazelle and other endangered animals. Its terrain is sandy plains with hills and valleys where natural grasses, seasonal herbs and wild trees grow among the dunes. According to its manager Mohammed Nasser Al Henzab, quoted in January 2025, the reserve holds around 1,000 oryx. It is one of 12 terrestrial and marine reserves that, with Umm Al Sheif approved at the end of 2024, cover about 25.73% of Qatar's territory, with a national goal of 30% by 2030 under the 2004 wildlife protection decree.
sites.sig: The largest single oryx herd reported in Qatar, and the breeding base for the country's gazelle and oryx reintroductions.

sites.s: Qatar's richest birding site · 238 species recorded
sites.te: Fodder fields full of birds
sites.se: Irrigated pivot fields on the Abu Samra road where 76% of all birds ever recorded in Qatar have been seen
sites.sa: حقول محورية مروية على طريق أبو سمرة شوهد فيها 76% من كل الطيور المسجلة في قطر
sites.desc: A fodder farm off the Abu Samra Road about 50 km west of Doha, in the south-central plain, watered by central-pivot irrigation on a flat sandy plain. By 2014, when a book on its fauna and flora was launched at the Ministry of Environment, 238 of the 315 bird species recorded in Qatar (76%) had been seen at Irkaya, more than anywhere else in the country, including 15 globally threatened species such as the sociable lapwing, and many of Qatar's 59 breeding species nest there. Native plants near the pivot run-off grow taller with larger leaves than in the open desert; birders report close to 250 species and a southern farm of roughly 15 km² with lagoons, reed beds and grassland. The Ministry now lists Erkia as a nature reserve on the migratory route of birds and insects, with a farm growing animal feed inside it.
sites.sig: Proof that a single irrigated farm can become the most important stopover for migratory birds on the peninsula.

sites.s: Artificial wetland of 9 km² south of Doha · flamingo flocks
sites.te: A lake made of waste water
sites.se: A treated-sewage reservoir since 1982 that became Qatar's biggest wetland and a flamingo haunt, then faced draining
sites.sa: خزان لمياه الصرف المعالجة منذ عام 1982 صار أكبر أرض رطبة في قطر ومقصدًا للنحام، ثم واجه التجفيف
sites.desc: An artificial wetland with natural topography about 12 km south of Doha near Abu Nakhla village, created in 1982 as a reservoir for treated sewage effluent from the Doha-South and Doha-West treatment stations, spread over nine square kilometres. At least 260 bird species have been recorded, with about 150 greater flamingos counted, frogs and fish in the pond, reeds and cat's-tail around it, and about 10% of Qatar's documented plant species in the area; the pond sits on the Simsima/Umm Bab and Midra Shale members of the Eocene Dammam Formation over a shallow aquifer, and a 2014–2015 study found low bacterial contamination and acceptable heavy-metal levels. In March 2014 the Public Works Authority Ashghal, under its president Nasser bin Ali al-Mawlawi, announced the lagoon would be drained by the end of that year; Qatar University's Anna Grichting Solder, who studied the site with her students, and Saif al-Hajri of Friends of the Environment argued in 2015 for an ecological wetland reserve with bio-drainage and bioremediation, noting the Ramsar secretariat and BirdLife International were ready to support a Ramsar listing, as Abu Dhabi's Al Wathba had received in 2013.
sites.sig: The largest wetland in Qatar, an accidental ecosystem that raised the question of what a desert city owes the birds it attracted.

sites.s: Seabird colony island off Doha · Important Bird Area
sites.te: Cormorants within sight of the towers
sites.se: A low coral-reef island north of The Pearl where Socotra cormorants and white-cheeked terns breed
sites.sa: جزيرة مرجانية منخفضة شمال اللؤلؤة يتكاثر فيها غاق سقطرى والخرشنة بيضاء الخد
sites.desc: A small, low-lying island off Al Daayen municipality north of The Pearl, 3.5 miles north of Al Safliya Island, with a brown surface and a small peak at its east end that once guided ships into Al Bidda harbour. Unlike Halul, which rests on ancient igneous and metamorphic rock, it is built of coral-reef structures, with loose weathered limestone, scattered Limonium and Zygophyllum bushes, a 2 km sandspit extending south at low tide and broad intertidal flats and coral reefs around it. BirdLife International designated it an Important Bird Area for its breeding colonies of Socotra cormorants and white-cheeked terns. The artificial island of The Pearl, built in the late 2000s, now lies between Al Aaliya and Al Safliya.
sites.sig: A breeding colony of the Gulf-endemic Socotra cormorant a few kilometres from Doha's skyline.

sites.s: Island park at Qatar's northern tip · hawksbill nesting
sites.el: One of 8 main turtle nesting sites · 219 turtles nested in 2025
sites.te: Mangroves at the top of the map
sites.se: Sand bars, islets and mangroves on an uninhabited island declared a national park in 2006
sites.sa: حواجز رملية وجزر صغيرة وقرم على جزيرة غير مأهولة أُعلنت حديقة وطنية عام 2006
sites.desc: A national park on an uninhabited island at the northern tip of Qatar, within 6.4 km of Ar Ruwais, established in 2006 during the 15th Asian Games. It has sand bars and small islets with mangroves, is a stopover for migratory birds on the Afro-Eurasian flyway and a nursery ground for fish and crustaceans, with dugong sightings in surrounding waters, and is one of the main hawksbill sea turtle nesting sites in the country. In the 2025 season, from 31 March to the end of July, the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change with QatarEnergy and Qatar University's Environmental Science Center recorded 219 nesting turtles across eight main sites including Umm Tais, Fuwairit, Ras Rakan, Ras Laffan and Al Ghariya, and released 8,213 hatchlings, bringing the project's five-year total to more than 60,000. The ruins of the old village of Al Mafjar lie nearby.

sites.n: National Museum of Qatar and the Palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani
sites.na: متحف قطر الوطني وقصر الشيخ عبدالله بن جاسم آل ثاني
sites.s: Desert-rose museum wrapped around a historic royal palace · UNESCO Tentative List 2025
sites.dr: UNESCO Tentative List, submitted 2 April 2025 (ref. 6815, criteria iv, vi)
sites.el: About 52,000 m² building; 1.5 km gallery route
sites.te: A desert rose that grew around a palace
sites.ta: وردة الصحراء التي نبتت حول قصر
sites.se: In Doha a museum shaped like a desert rose wraps around the old palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim and tells Qatar’s story along a 1.5 km path
sites.sa: في الدوحة يلتفّ متحف على هيئة وردة الصحراء حول القصر القديم للشيخ عبدالله بن جاسم، ويروي قصة قطر على مسار طوله 1.5 كيلومتر
sites.desc: The National Museum of Qatar in Doha surrounds the restored historic Palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani (1880–1957), son of the founder of modern Qatar. The original national museum was founded in 1975; the new building by Jean Nouvel, based on the form of the desert rose and built of large interlocking disks, opened on 28 March 2019. The building covers about 52,000 m², and eleven permanent galleries form a 1.5 km route through Qatar’s history, natural environment and cultural change. Qatar submitted it to the UNESCO Tentative List on 2 April 2025 under criteria (iv) and (vi).

sites.n: Al Ruwais Pleistocene sea cow fossil site
sites.na: موقع أحفورة الأطوم البليستوسينية في الرويس
sites.s: Last-interglacial beach deposit · fossil sea cow rib
sites.dr: Futaisi Member, Fuwayrit Formation; about 125 ka (inferred, MIS 5e)
sites.te: A sea cow on a 125,000-year-old beach
sites.ta: بقرة بحر على شاطئ عمره 125 ألف عام
sites.se: On the shore west of Al Ruwais, rocks from an ancient beach held the rib of a sea cow that grazed seagrass about 125,000 years ago
sites.sa: على الساحل غرب الرويس حفظت صخور شاطئ قديم ضلعًا لبقرة بحر كانت ترعى الأعشاب البحرية قبل نحو 125 ألف عام
sites.desc: A shoreline outcrop west of Al Ruwais in northern Qatar exposes the Futaisi Member of the Fuwayrit Formation, the earliest Pleistocene deposit preserved on the Qatar peninsula. The member is no more than 1 m thick and reaches about 1.5 m above present high tide: a basal lag of dolomite pebbles is overlain by cross-bedded oolitic grainstone with burrows, read as a wave-dominated foreshore to upper shoreface deposit from a Pleistocene sea-level highstand. In December 2019 a dugongid rib fragment (QM.2021.0504), about 112 mm long, was collected here; it most resembles the living dugong. Its age of about 125 ka is inferred by correlation with last-interglacial (MIS 5e) platforms, not by direct dating.
sites.sig: A fossil sea cow from Qatar’s earliest preserved Pleistocene deposit, showing that seagrass meadows and dugong-like animals were in the Arabian Gulf by about 125,000 years ago.

sites.s: Prehistoric flint workshops on a coastal rock ridge · 41 tanged points at one spot
sites.p: Prehistoric (described as Mesolithic by the excavator)
sites.dr: Investigated 1959 by the Danish expedition; published 1961
sites.te: The ridge where hunters made arrowheads
sites.ta: التلّ الذي صنع فيه الصيادون رؤوس سهامهم
sites.se: On a low rock ridge north of Doha, early hunters camped out of the wind and left thousands of flint chips and arrowheads
sites.sa: على تلّ صخري منخفض شمال الدوحة احتمى صيادون قدماء من الرياح، وتركوا آلاف الشظايا ورؤوس السهام من الصوان
sites.desc: Al Wusail is a rock ridge on Qatar’s east coast about 25 km north of Doha, running NNW–SSE about 600–700 m inland, about 1 km long and 150–200 m wide. In 1959 Danish archaeologist Viggo Nielsen found flint at 12 localities on the ridge, six of which he considered habitation sites. Locality 2, where 61 m² were examined, yielded about 5,000–6,000 flint pieces, including 41 tanged points, about 85 blades and scrapers. Nielsen found no close parallels in Qatar and placed the industry in a general Mesolithic setting.
sites.sig: Studied by the Danish expedition in 1959, it shows early people using a sheltered coastal ridge near grazing game.

refs: Nielsen, V. (1961). Al Wusail. Mesolitiske flintpladser i Qatar [Al Wusail: Mesolithic flint sites in Qatar]. Kuml 11, 169–184. https://doi.org/10.7146/kuml.v11i11.103350

sites.sa: بجوار سوق واقف تقف قلعة الكوت، التي كانت مخفرًا وسجنًا، وصارت اليوم متحفًا للحرف القطرية القديمة
sites.desc: Al Koot Fort is a historic military fortress in the Al Bidda area of Doha, within Souq Waqif near the Corniche. Sources date it to 1880 and record that it was rebuilt in 1927 under Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani, who ruled from 1913 to 1949. It served as a police station, as a jail from 1906, and as a military fort from 1927 to 1977. Renovated in 1978, it became a museum of traditional handicrafts, fishing equipment, boats and historical photographs.
sites.sig: A surviving fortress of old Doha whose changing uses, from jail and fort to museum, trace the city’s modern history.

sites.s: Neolithic coastal settlement of about 6000 BC · lost and found again in 2015
sites.el: Shagra II path about 18 m long with 4–5 dwellings

sites.se: Near Al Wakrah, a Stone Age fishing village of stone houses was lost for decades, then found again with a second village nearby

sites.desc: Shagra is a Neolithic site in Al Wakrah municipality, dated to about 6000 BC, first found by a French archaeological team in 1981 and described by Marie-Louise Inizan in 1988. Finds include a two-room structure, flints and the remains of fish and molluscs. After Qatar Museums Authority could not relocate it in 2010–2012, geologist Jacques LeBlanc rediscovered the site in 2015 and found Shagra II about 0.65 km to the north-west. Shagra II has a path about 18 m long with the foundations of four to five adjacent dwellings, further dwellings nearby and a possible child’s grave set in sabkha.
sites.sig: A Neolithic settlement with house foundations in south-east Qatar, showing coastal people living on fish and shellfish about 8,000 years ago.

sites.s: West-coast sabkha where microbial mats help make dolomite · Holocene
sites.dr: Holocene evaporitic sabkha with living microbial mats
sites.el: About 109 Mg of carbon per hectare
sites.te: Where microbes build rock
sites.se: On Qatar’s west coast, slimy mats of microbes in a salt flat help grow dolomite, a rock that is hard to make anywhere else today
sites.sa: على الساحل الغربي لقطر تساعد حُصُر لزجة من الميكروبات في سبخة ملحية على تكوين الدولوميت، وهو صخر يصعب أن يتكوّن في أي مكان آخر اليوم
sites.desc: Dohat Faishakh is a coastal sabkha on the north-west coast of the Qatar peninsula whose sediments, dominated by gypsum and carbonate minerals, formed during the Holocene and are covered with microbial mats. Cores DF1–DF4 showed that dolomite forms not only in the evaporitic supratidal zone but also within microbial mats in the lower intertidal zone, closely tied to the mats’ extracellular polymeric substances, pointing to a microbially influenced process. Porewater salinity ranged from 140 to 310‰, and sediment carbon stocks averaged about 109.1 ± 7.1 Mg C per hectare, higher than at Khor Al Adaid sabkha (67.8) and above the soil carbon of Qatari mangroves.
sites.sig: A natural laboratory for how dolomite, a major reservoir rock of the Arabian Gulf region, can form at low temperature with the help of microbes.

sites.s: Cliffs near Dukhan that serve as Qatar’s reference section for its Eocene rocks
sites.el: About 26 m of exposed Rus Formation
sites.te: Pages of an ancient sea
sites.se: In low cliffs near Dukhan, layers of limestone, marl and shale record the warm shallow sea that covered Qatar about 50 million years ago
sites.sa: في جروف منخفضة قرب دخان تسجّل طبقات الحجر الجيري والمارل والطَّفل البحر الدافئ الضحل الذي غطّى قطر قبل نحو 50 مليون عام
sites.desc: Cliffs about 1 km east of the Fahahil plant near Dukhan form the Qatar reference section described by Cavelier (1970) for the country’s surface Eocene rocks. About 26 m of the Rus Formation is exposed: whitish, soft, variably dolomitised limestone and green to brown dolomitic marl, with chert and quartz geodes near the base. Above it the section shows the base of the Dammam Formation, with the full Alveolina Bed, the Midra Shale Member and the bottom of the Umm Bab Member. The Rus is Early Eocene (Ypresian, about 56–48.9 Ma) and the Dammam Early to Middle Eocene, ending about 41.4 Ma.
sites.sig: The standard surface section against which Qatar’s two main Eocene formations, also its main aquifer rocks, are described.

sites.desc: Simaisma is a coastal settlement on the east coast of Qatar, between Doha and Al Khor. In 1908 Lorimer’s Gazetteer described it as a walled village of about 250 families with 50 pearl boats, drawing drinking water from wells at Uwaynat bin Hussain. Its mosque, built in 1938, is one of the oldest surviving mosques in Qatar and once housed a madrasa. Archaeological work in the area by the Qatar National Historic Environment Record team, and a Qatar Museums excavation of an inhumation at Aerospace City north of Smaisma, have recorded burials; Wikipedia, citing Cuttler (2014), reports two circular burial mounds dated to the 5th century BC.

sites.dr: Built 1935; courtyard wall rebuilt 2015; Qatar Museums heritage site
sites.te: The little mosque among the towers
sites.se: Built in 1935 when the land around it was open, this small mosque now hides among Doha’s tall buildings, its old minaret still standing
sites.sa: بُني عام 1935 حين كانت الأرض من حوله فضاءً مفتوحًا، وهو اليوم مسجد صغير يختبئ بين أبنية الدوحة الشاهقة، ومئذنته القديمة ما زالت قائمة
sites.desc: A traditional neighbourhood mosque in Doha, originally built in 1935 in an open area and now surrounded by large modern buildings in a commercial district. It consists of a courtyard and a prayer hall: ten ornamented openings separate the outer prayer hall from the courtyard, three doors lead to the inner prayer hall, and the mihrab is semicircular with a pointed dome. The original cylindrical minaret, about 5 m tall, stands at the south-east corner of the courtyard on a round base, with a dome carried on six columns. In 2015 the courtyard wall was rebuilt and a house for the imam and a new ablution area were added.
sites.sig: One of the few surviving pre-oil neighbourhood mosques of old Doha, conserved by Qatar Museums.
